newsitem.title: USA: Perot seeks court-enforced entry into U.S. debates.
newsitem.headline: Perot seeks court-enforced entry into U.S. debates.

text.p: Reform Party presidential nominee Ross Perot filed suit on Monday to force his way into campaign debates between President Bill Clinton and Republican nominee Bob Dole.

Lawyers for Perot and his running mate, economist Pat Choate, filed papers in U.S. District Court in Washington seeking an injunction to force their inclusion in presidential and vice presidential debates scheduled for next month.

The lawyers said they hoped a judge would hold a hearing on their suit this week. They would argue that Perot's constitutional rights were violated when the Commission on Presidential Debates decided the Texas billionaire should not be included because he had no chance of being elected.
That recommendation was effectively accepted by the Clinton and Dole camps when they agreed on final debate terms -- excluding Perot -- last weekend.
"Declaring the election essentially over for all candidates but two before a single debate takes place will only deepen the nation's cynicism about government," the lawsuit said.

The Dole and Clinton camps agreed to hold two one-on-one televised presidential debates between their candidates on October 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, and October 16 in San Diego, California. A vice presidential debate was scheduled for October 9 in St. Petersburg, Florida.
Clinton, who had originally backed Perot's demand to participate, told reporters at a White House bill-signing ceremony that Perot's exclusion was Dole's fault.

"We signed an agreement with the Dole campaign when it was obvious there would be no debate if Mr. Perot was involved," he said. "And I thought the American people were entitled to a debate between Senator Dole and me. So i told the people who were negotiating for me to go ahead and sign the agreement."

The Perot camp has portrayed the move as an establishment effort to smother a third-party candidate who won 19 percent of the popular vote in the 1992 presidential election after making a strong mark in that year's debates.

"We are here this morning because there is no more fundamental exercise of free speech in this country than the right to vote for the candidate of your choice," Perot campaign spokesman Russell Verney told reporters at the court.
He said a Louis Harris poll found that 76 percent of voters want Perot included in the debates as he was in 1992.

Perot's suit named the Federal Election Commission, which oversees campaign financing laws but has not been involved in debate preparations, as the agency that should be directed to have the Reform Party candidates included. The suit argues that the debate commission, a privately funded agency established by the two major parties in the 1980s to organise the debates, is a fraudulent entity.

"The Republicans and Democrats have joined to get them (the FEC) to put up a fraudulent front organisation, the Commission on Presidential Debates, to control the debates and keep third-party candidates out of the debates," Verney said.

The commission recommended last week that Perot should not be invited because it felt he had no realistic chance of winning. Current opinion polls show him garnering only five or six percent backing, with Clinton solidly in the lead and Dole his only close competition.
The Dole camp opposed Perot's inclusion all along because it sees him as more a threat to their candidate than Clinton.
Perot has since treated Dole and the commission to the withering sarcastic tongue-lashings that are his hallmark.

"Now here is a guy who is supposed to be a war hero," he said of Dole, a decorated and combat-wounded veteran of World War II, in an NBC interview on Sunday. "You'd think he'd be willing to talk to another person, wouldn't you?"

Perot argues that the debate commission -- which did invite him into the 1992 presidential campaign debates, where he aimed most of his fire at Clinton's rival, then-President George Bush -- does the bidding of the two major parties,
